description:
We are a team of passionate students from ElSewedy University of Technology, interested in AI, Data Science, Programming, and Space Technology.

Our goal is to develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA’s open data.

We welcome creative and motivated students with skills in programming, AI, data analysis, UI/UX design, and problem-solving. 🚀
summary:
ASTRA // Orbital EVA OS is a real-time health monitoring system and 3D digital twin for astronauts during spacewalks (EVA). We developed a Python backend and a Three.js dashboard that tracks heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2), skin temperature, suit pressure and neutron radiation dose for each crew member, using simulated telemetry based on NASA's Risks of Human Spaceflight and radiation monitoring resources.

An AI co-pilot compares vitals against each astronaut's personal baseline, predicts drift toward danger 30 seconds ahead, and detects hypoxia, suit leaks, heat stress, radiation exposure and cumulative dose limits. It also separates real medical problems from sensor failures. When something goes wrong, ASTRA raises an alert, generates an incident report and recommends actions such as deploying shielding or boosting oxygen. A smart ring gives haptic warnings, and role-based access lets astronauts, doctors and admins see what they need.

This matters because on long missions with delayed communication with Earth, astronauts need early warning and autonomous decision support to stay safe.
details:
1) Startup

  1. You run demo2.py. It starts the server on 127.0.0.1:8050 and opens the browser automatically.
  2. It sets up a SQLite database with a table of astronauts (amira, lukas, yuki, each with a cumulative dose), an alerts table, and a users table. It also creates default accounts (user / doctor / admin) and prints them to the console.
  3. It starts a background worker thread and the AI.
  4. The server serves index.html, style.css and app.js from the static folder.

2) What the server does every second

The worker loops over every astronaut and runs step_simulation once per second:

  1. Reads the current scenario for that astronaut from the database. Each scenario has target values. For example, Suit Leak targets a heart rate of 154, SpO2 of 86% and suit pressure of 2.75 PSI.
  2. Applies fixes if they were pressed. Shielding returns neutron dose to 5.4, O2 Purge restores oxygen and pressure, and Cooling returns temperature to 36.5.
  3. Moves values gradually toward the target (ease_state), so a value drops or rises over about 30 seconds (radiation reacts about 5x faster). It then adds small random noise to look realistic.
  4. Generates a simulated PPG signal (260 samples, red and IR) containing a pulse at the current heart rate.
  5. Analyzes the signal (analyze_ppg): removes the baseline, smooths it, finds peaks, computes heart rate from the peak spacing, and computes SpO2 from the ratio between the two signals. If no pulse is found, it returns signal_ok = False.
  6. Updates the cumulative dose based on neutron rate and saves it to the database.
  7. Stores the result (HR, SpO2, temp, psi, neutron, cumulative dose) in LAST and sends it to the AI (AI.push).

3) What the AI does with each reading

  1. Checks for faults. Impossible values (e.g. heart rate 300) are classified as a sensor fault and ignored. If the PPG signal is lost 3 times in a row, heart rate and SpO2 are ignored.
  2. Smooths the latest readings.
  3. Applies clinical rules (assess). For example, SpO2 below 92 is a warning and below 88 is critical. Pressure below 3.5 is a warning and below 3.0 is critical.
  4. Predicts the future. After at least 10 samples, it computes the trend of each vital, predicts its value 30 seconds ahead, and converts the distance to the alert limit into a risk score from 0 to 1.
  5. Compares to a personal baseline. If a value moves far from that astronaut’s normal (4 standard deviations), it is logged as an anomaly. While everything is healthy, the baseline slowly updates.
  6. Determines the condition (Suit Leak, Heat Stress, Radiation, etc.) and picks the cause and recommended actions from the Playbook.
  7. Incidents. When a finding reaches warning level or higher, it opens an Incident Report, keeps updating it (worst values, timeline), closes it after 8 seconds of healthy data, and saves it to astra_incidents.jsonl.
  8. Watchdog. A second thread watches for silence. If no data arrives for 5 seconds, it declares “Telemetry Lost”.

4) What happens in the browser

  1. On load, app.js calls /api/me. If you are not logged in, the login screen appears.
  2. After login, permissions are applied to the interface: scenario buttons are locked for non-admins, fix buttons are locked for doctors, and astronauts see only themselves.
  3. Every second (setInterval) it calls /api/state/<astronaut> to get vitals, AI analysis and the PPG waveform. It also calls /api/ai/crew to color the crew dropdown with 🟢🟡🟠🔴 status icons and show the alert banner.
  4. It updates the HUD: values, panel colors (red on alert), the AI toast at the bottom (NORMAL / WARNING / CRITICAL / PREDICTIVE for early warnings), and the status dot at the top.
  5. ASTRA-Ring: during an alert the ring shakes and turns red or amber, and the ring and suit in the 3D scene change color too.
  6. The 3D scene (Three.js) runs in requestAnimationFrame (about 60 times per second), independent of the polling.

5) Full example: Suit Leak scenario

  1. The admin clicks Suit Leak, and the browser sends PUT /api/crew/amira/scenario.
  2. The server updates the scenario in the database.
  3. Over the next seconds, pressure falls from 4.30 toward 2.75, oxygen from 98.6 toward 86, and heart rate climbs.
  4. After about 10 seconds the AI notices the trend and shows a PREDICTIVE early warning, before any limit is crossed.
  5. Pressure crosses 3.5, so a warning fires, an Incident Report opens, and a red banner appears saying “HEALTH WARNING” with a View report button.
  6. The O2 Pressure Purge button lights up. When the astronaut or admin presses it, PUT .../overrides is sent.
  7. Values return gradually to normal. After 8 healthy seconds the incident closes, and the report stays available to copy or download.
